qa.question: Why does this fit a source-limit framework?
qa.answer: The public story stabilized before full laboratory certainty, and people relied on visible sequence markers instead of complete mechanistic proof.

qa.answer: The pump handle was removed during the outbreak after pattern-based evidence supported a concentrated source hypothesis.

longformArticle.deck: The Broad Street cholera event became a durable model for how old wells and shared sources enter legend when records are partial and actions happen faster than proof.
opening: The 1854 Soho outbreak produced a compact incident record: a named source, disputed mechanism, mapped cases, and a visible intervention.
This one chain is why old-well stories often persist as cultural memory even after technical certainty increases.

storyBody.heading: Soho and the Old Well Setting
paragraphs: The event began in Soho, where a single public pump was a practical daily resource in a crowded district.
Before intervention, residents and officials worked with incomplete causal proof, and the shared source became the easiest focal point for concern.
That made the site narratively heavy before scientific confidence had stabilized.

storyBody.heading: Outbreak and Competing Early Explanations
paragraphs: The 1854 outbreak arrived in a context where miasma explanations still held influence, so initial interpretations were contested.
A high concentration of cases around the Broad Street area did not automatically prove mechanism; it created a pressure point for competing claims.

storyBody.heading: Household-Level Recording and Map Reconstruction
paragraphs: John Snow and collaborators documented illness locations and water-use patterns, then organized them into a geographically structured account.
Household-level detail, not just general rumor, shifted the event from broad panic toward a source-aware sequence.
The resulting pattern made the Broad Street pump a singular explanatory node in public discussion.

storyBody.heading: Handle Removal and Public-Health Action
paragraphs: Authorities removed the pump handle in response to the mapped pattern and emerging source concerns.
The action signaled a practical shift: control the suspicious source first, then continue evidence work.
Even without perfect certainty, the source-control move made the timeline physically visible in the community.

storyBody.heading: After-Effect and Enduring Narrative Power
paragraphs: The immediate event subsided as intervention and scrutiny intensified, but the sequence remained in print, teaching, and memory cycles.
Later public-health history recast the event as foundational, while legend form preserved the simpler story: one source, one crisis, one decisive act.
That retention is the narrative aftereffect of source-limited records.

storyBody.heading: Why Old Wells Carry Source-Limit Legends
paragraphs: Old wells and public pumps are materially specific; even limited evidence can lock onto them as anchors.
When records are sparse, the public tends to preserve the source object and sequence even while interpretations evolve.
This explains why well stories repeatedly outlive their initial medical setting and become broader cautionary folklore.
